pr.title: Preserve caches in a call to shrink_to_fit
pr.description: A small follow up to rust-lang/rust#142542.
pr.author: tmiasko

processing.reason: The PR is a cache-preservation cleanup, not a semantics-changing miscompilation. `simplify_cfg` returns `()`, and the only change is replacing `body.basic_blocks_mut().raw.shrink_to_fit()` with `body.basic_blocks.as_mut_preserves_cfg().shrink_to_fit()`. Both calls shrink the same raw basic-block vector after `remove_dead_blocks`; the difference is solely whether a derived CFG cache is invalidated. Invalidation discards/recomputes cached data but does not alter MIR/CFG contents or observable program behavior, so there is no concrete input on which the original and transformed functions yield different program values. The patch explicitly adds no regression test, and the frozen analysis notes ordinary MIR-output tests cannot distinguish the revisions. Constructing a Body/cache simulation that prints a boolean “cache preserved” value would invent an observation and return-value change not present in the historical function, which the task forbids as forcing a difference. Therefore no source-grounded semantic counterexample pair can be validated.

analysis.originalLogic: In `simplify_cfg`, after `remove_dead_blocks(body)`, the pass intentionally shrinks the basic-block storage while preserving the CFG: `body.basic_blocks.as_mut_preserves_cfg().shrink_to_fit();`. This keeps any CFG-derived caches valid because shrinking capacity does not change CFG structure.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historically incorrect code used the general mutable basic-block accessor: `body.basic_blocks_mut().raw.shrink_to_fit();`. Although this still shrinks the raw basic-block vector, it goes through the cache-invalidating mutable path. The PR replaces it with `body.basic_blocks.as_mut_preserves_cfg().shrink_to_fit();`, preserving caches when only allocation capacity, not CFG edges, is changed.
analysis.inputDomain: MIR bodies processed by the `SimplifyCfg` pass after `remove_dead_blocks`, where `body.basic_blocks` has excess allocation capacity and CFG-derived caches may be populated. The distinction is which `Body` basic-block accessor is used for a capacity-only operation, not the shape of the input program's control flow.
analysis.summary: Historical SimplifyCfg change preserves CFG caches when shrinking basic-block storage after dead-block removal. The reusable invariant is that capacity-only operations on MIR basic blocks must use the accessor that preserves CFG-derived caches rather than the general mutable accessor, which invalidates them.
analysis.trigger: Calling `shrink_to_fit()` on MIR basic-block storage at the end of `SimplifyCfg` after dead blocks have been removed.
preconditions: The `SimplifyCfg` pass has run `remove_dead_blocks(body)` and is only reclaiming excess capacity.
No CFG edges or block contents are being changed by the shrink operation.
The caller can use the CFG-preserving mutable accessor.
pitfalls: Do not treat a capacity-only `shrink_to_fit` like a structural CFG mutation.
Using `basic_blocks_mut()` unnecessarily discards cache state even though the CFG is unchanged.
Conversely, do not use `as_mut_preserves_cfg()` for operations that actually mutate CFG structure.

This PR contains no regression test, and no compiler execution or reproduction was performed, so any test must explicitly assert cache preservation or allocation behavior rather than infer it from ordinary MIR output.
analysis.testStrategy: Use a compiler-internal unit/regression test that inspects or instruments the CFG cache around `SimplifyCfg` after `remove_dead_blocks`, or asserts the basic-block allocation capacity shrinks while cached CFG data remains usable. Because the patch adds no test, ordinary MIR-output tests would not distinguish the two transformations; they differ in cache state, not semantic output. A build/test claim must be based on actually running such a test, which was not done here.
evidence: Preserve caches in a call to shrink_to_fit
